title: Caribbean Horizon Estate, Saint Lucia
concept: A composed hilltop estate arranged as a deep, two-storey sea-facing U: a substantial protected residence forms a calm court open to the Caribbean horizon, while a detached horizon pavilion sits to the east as a lower, independent destination. The architecture is deliberately horizontal and grounded, using a broad plinth-like main mass to make the sea, sky and sheltered outdoor rooms feel dominant rather than competing with a vertical object.
character: Sculptural Caribbean modernism: weighty, shade-casting horizontal volumes, a protected wind-tempered court, and a restrained procession from the landward south to the open northern sea edge.
decisions: The principal residence is a 46 by 32 metre articulated U-shaped envelope, with a 14 metre-deep northern recess. Its substantial southern bar anchors the estate against the landward approach while two 7.8 metre-deep side wings frame the sea.
The U opens north toward the assumed Caribbean view, creating a 30 by 14 metre sheltered sea court. This court is a true exterior void in the building mass rather than an enclosed internal courtyard.
The residence rises two generous storeys, giving it enough presence for the estate while retaining a low, horizon-oriented profile.
A flat roof consolidates the non-rectangular main volume as one calm horizontal datum and emphasizes the cut-out geometry of the sea court.

A detached eastern horizon pavilion is set beyond a narrow landscape gap from the main wing. Its distinct rectangular volume avoids making the estate read as a single oversized block and gives the seaward edge a secondary architectural focal point.
The horizon pavilion receives a butterfly roof, making its silhouette visibly independent from the flat-roofed residence without exceeding the main house in scale.
The southern arrival is held apart from the residence by a formal outdoor arrival court, slowing the transition from landward entry to the protected central composition.
A broad northern panorama terrace is separated from the house by planted ground, preserving the court as an intimate sheltered exterior while establishing a larger, open-air sea outlook.
assumptions: The site is an approximately 100 by 90 metre private Saint Lucia parcel with the Caribbean Sea and principal long view to the north.
The selected building zone is treated as flat ground; the requested overlooking condition is understood as a naturally elevated coastal setting beyond the modelled plinth elevations.
Landscape, retaining terrain, access drives, planting and water elements are outside this massing concept and are not represented as constructed geometry.
The estate is intended as a private luxury residence with a separate seaward pavilion, rather than a multi-building resort compound.
